en: And all your strongest men come without mercy
To seize Külchoro!
Come, you wolves never sated with blood;
Let your most capable men
Charge the warrior head-on
And capture him alive.
Plunge Külchoro
Into misery so deep he cannot escape;
Subject the wretch
To merciless torment.
Bind both his hands
And hamstring him.
Do not kill him or let him vanish;
Take vengeance as heavy as a mattock.
Hollow out his right shoulder,
And flay his left shoulder!”
Make him the lowly slave
Of some sixty herdsmen,
Fetching their firewood and water.
Morning and evening, twice a day,
Stretch him out and beat him like a hide.
Deliver punishment with your own hands
Upon this slave who calls himself a hero!
Do not kill him quickly;
Kill him through humiliation
And give him his punishment!
Your valiant Khan Kyyaz,
Surge in and enter;
Take the monstrous warrior
As your spoil!”
Against the warrior in the cave,
The lion favored by fate,
The hero lying helpless
With ninety wounds,
The Jediger closed in from every side,
Loosing their bows like rain
And shooting arrows like hail.
From every direction
Came shouting men with leveled spears.
All those shouting
Raised the battle cry “Kyyaz!”
Their bows rained shafts,
Their arrows fell like hail,
And the Jediger swept inside.
Then Külchoro,
His strength spent and power gone,
His whole body drained of blood,
Was burning inside and out,
His entrails aflame with fire.
He had the soul of a champion in battle,
But the wretched warrior was helpless.
His eyes alone stared pleadingly,
His joints had failed and hung limp;
His vigor was spent, his strength gone,
His face pale from loss of blood.
All power had left Külchoro.
As the champions surged upon him
And encircled him,
About to plunge him into bitter misery,
He grasped Joykuma, his khan-father’s sword,
By the hilt,
Drew it from its sheath,
Swung it in his grip,
And hewed fifty champions
Clean apart.
Those farther away
He made crawl beneath his spear,
And those who came nearer
He toyed with upon his sword.
The famed lionhearted hero
Whirled about in fury,
Hurling every champion he seized
Like a blue-gray kid.
He crushed all who faced him—
Where now were their brave men?
He smashed all who approached—
Where now were their tigers?
Warrior Külchoro kept them at bay,
Refusing to submit
To the Jediger’s violence.
Külchoro would not surrender
His fly-like soul to that host.
Hero Kyyaz of the Jediger
Came thrusting with his spear,
Intent on binding Külchoro;
Firing his gun and loosing his bow,
He drove resolutely in.
Wearing a coat like a mountain’s ash,
Riding his swift bay stallion,
He tied up short the streaming tail
Of his restless sorrel horse.
Burning with eagerness, hero Kyyaz
Charged against the warrior.
When you looked upon Külchoro,
The breath from his mouth
Was like the wind through a mountain valley,
As though it would devour whoever faced him.
His strength was beyond compare.
When you looked upon the fierce warrior,
His courage was just as extraordinary:
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
A fierce man resembling a lion,
He leveled his spear wherever battle raged.
The champions who clashed with him
Craved a patch of ground as small as a hare’s.
He did not flinch when a gun was fired,
And when they closed in combat,
He did not fearfully leave his flank exposed.
His tigerish eyes blazed,
And he bit his lips until they split.
When he turned and looked you in the face,
He seemed the very mold of seasoned warriors.
The wind issuing from his mouth
Was like a tempest from Bukhara;
The fury of his two eyes
Was like embers in a riverbed,
And when he muttered, his voice
Was like the shot of a cannon.
When one looked before him,
A black-maned tiger
Seemed poised to tear open a wound;
A black-striped tiger
Crouched directly in front
Of this ill-fated man,
While a devouring dragon,
Its jaws gaping cavernously,
Crouched behind him.
The giant Zümrük bird
Seemed ready to swoop down at once,
Its talons stretched wide.
He wheeled like a tiger,
And none who grappled with him survived.
His wrathful aspect was unlike any other,
Overawing the whole wide world.
The renowned master of battle,
His quiver curved like the waist of a maiden,
Was a raging black calamity
That seemed ready to devour any foe.
His appearance was strange, his venom strong;
If you met him, you abandoned hope of life.
Such was his form:
Broad-chested, with expansive shoulders,
Wide-mouthed and beetle-browed,
Broad-browed and deep-eyed—
Thus had the Creator made the warrior.
Taking a mace as large as a house,
He scowled and raised havoc.
He struck a black rock once,
Sparks bursting from his mace
And fire leaping from the stone.
In the close-fought struggle
He never fearfully exposed his flank,
And of the champions who faced him
He crushed many into the earth.
When Kyyaz saw Külchoro,
He could not endure his heat
Or withstand his cold;
He could not advance to confront him
Or plant his spear firmly.
Turning his back, hero Kyyaz
Could not bear it and withdrew.
He wheeled his horse and fled;
When he saw the warrior’s might,
He could not turn back and wreak havoc,
But pleaded with Kanchoro:
“My dear comrade,
Your lifelong companion Külchoro
Is blessed with perfect fortune.
Look into the heart of this matter—
Good heavens, comrade, consider it!
He is a son destined to be a fortress
For the eagle of the yellow bluff,
A son destined to be a shield
Not merely for the Kyrgyz, but for all the ages.
He is a peerless, valiant hero.
His very form sets him apart from all others,
He is both a hero and a man of bitter fate,
A true man would not dare lay hands on him;
He is a genuinely born hero.
I marveled when I saw his stature—
No other soul like him will be born.
No one facing him has ever struck,
No man has ever dared grapple with the hero.
This truly born Külchoro—
Can anyone who tangles with him prosper?
Against this sacred warrior,
Look—can one who attacks him survive?
For these blessed Kyrgyz
He was born to be their guardian;
For these perfectly formed Kyrgyz
He was born to be their khan;
When enraged against the enemy,
He is a son whose torrent overwhelms them.
For this small, ancient Kyrgyz nation
He was born to be its backbone.
This dark-fated hero—
Seen from the front, he brings good fortune;
Seen from behind, he seems an army countless strong.
His radiant beauty is an omen of fortune,
His wolf-like valor equals countless troops;
His muscles are thick as a man’s waist,
And when he surges, he seems ready to devour a soul.
His strength is like tempered iron,
And when he charges, he seems ready to devour a soul;
His majesty is like a towering cliff,
And when he grapples, he seems ready to devour a soul.
His heart is steel, his outer frame is bronze—
What man could ever stand against him?
When fury seizes and maddens him,
He darts like ten striking snakes;
His combat blazes like red-hot coals—
What wrestler could withstand him?
Would anyone dare face him in battle?
Would anyone he attacks remain alive?
When enraged, he cannot be restrained;
No man he pursues can escape.
My bosom friend, listen to my words:
The two reins and the single bridle—
I yield them to you, my friend; take command.
Against this hero raging in fury,
You yourself must wage the battle.
This handful of the Jediger—
Would there be sin or merit in destroying them?
Take the duty upon yourself;
Hero, wage the battle yourself.
He is the enemy whose secrets you know;
My friend, deal with him as you know best.
Hero, do not stir up
Any needless quarrel.
My lion, whose cunning is complete,
Devise the means to deal with him yourself.
The Jediger will face a true slaughter—
Hero, bind him with your own hands.
Your hero’s courage is unmatched, his venom fierce;
If you do not act as you see fit,
My dearest friend,
He will level every one of us.
If you mean to kill him, kill him yourself;
Hero, if you mean to bind him, bind him yourself!
Hero, use all your cunning.
Do not think I shrink from combat;
Hero, restrain your anger.
Here stand the Kyrgyz people with their chiefs;
If you would cut off my head, here I stand.
This slave of yours has driven me into a frenzy;
Hero, if you would kill me, here is the ground.
Hero, if you are enraged, here is your chance.
Let me offer before you
This fleet bay racehorse as a gift.
Hero, if you bear a grudge, here are my people;
If you would sever my head,
Here am I, your precious Kyyaz!
Hero, as Kanchoro you have prospered—
Külchoro and Kanchoro,
You two grew up as equals.
You are confidants raised side by side;
